prompt: A web server queries a database to build the page it was asked for. In the exchange with the database, the web server is:
hint: Look at who started that particular exchange.

choices.text: the server, since that is what it is
choices.why: Its part in the browser's exchange does not carry over into this one.

choices.text: the client, since it did the asking
choices.why: Whoever starts an exchange is its client, whatever it was a moment ago.

choices.text: both, since it holds two exchanges
choices.why: It holds two roles across two exchanges, but one part in each of them.

choices.text: undecided, until the query comes back
choices.why: The part is fixed the moment it asks. Waiting is what a client does.

prompt: Which sentence uses "server" to mean the ROLE rather than the program or the machine?
hint: Ask whether the thing named could play a different part in the next exchange.

choices.text: "The build failed on the server we rent in Frankfurt."
choices.why: A thing with a location you rent is the hardware sense.

choices.text: "Restart the server; it stopped answering an hour ago."
choices.why: A thing you restart is a process — the program sense.

choices.text: "When the API reads the user record, the database serves it."
choices.why: It names the part something plays in one exchange, which is the role.

choices.text: "Our server runs eight containers and a reverse proxy."
choices.why: A thing that runs containers is a machine, not a part in a conversation.

prompt: A colleague says a phone cannot be a server. Which of these are reasons that claim is wrong? Choose all that apply.
hint: Separate what the role requires from what a large deployment requires.

choices.text: The role asks only for an address and a program that waits
choices.why: Those two properties are the whole of what the role requires.

choices.text: A phone can hold an address and run a program that listens
choices.why: Which is exactly what makes something the answering side.

choices.text: Size decides how many askers it can hold, not which part it plays
choices.why: Capacity and role are different questions about the same machine.

choices.text: A phone answers requests from its own apps all the time
choices.why: Apps on a phone mostly ask outward; this is not what makes the claim wrong.

choices.text: Phones are given fixed addresses by their mobile network
choices.why: They are usually not, and that difficulty is real — it is just not the point here.

prompt: Which of these belong to the CLIENT's side of an exchange? Choose all that apply.
hint: One side moves first; the other is found.

choices.text: Waiting to be spoken to before anything happens
choices.why: Waiting is the answering side's behaviour.

choices.text: Choosing the subject of the request
choices.why: The asker decides what is being asked about.

choices.text: Sitting at an address the other side can look up
choices.why: Being findable is what the answering side must be.

choices.text: Starting the exchange in the first place
choices.why: Asking first is what makes something the client.

choices.text: Deciding to walk away before the answer lands
choices.why: Nothing obliges an asker to wait, which is why cancel works.

prompt: A printer on the office network accepts print jobs, and every hour it reports its toner level to a monitoring system. How are its roles best described?
hint: Count the exchanges, and ask who started each one.

choices.text: A server for print jobs and a client when it reports
choices.why: It is asked for one and it does the asking for the other — one part per exchange.

choices.text: A client throughout, because it is not a computer
choices.why: The role never follows from what kind of equipment something is.

choices.text: A server throughout, because it sits and waits
choices.why: It waits for print jobs and starts the toner report, which is a different part.

choices.text: Neither, because a printer is a peripheral
choices.why: Anything addressable that asks or answers is playing one of the two parts.

prompt: The router in your home is best described as which of these?
hint: Ask whether you ever send it a request that it answers.

choices.text: An endpoint, since requests are addressed to it
choices.why: An endpoint answers requests; this passes them on to somewhere else.

choices.text: A host, because it has an address of its own
choices.why: It does have one, and holding nothing you visit is what keeps it out of the category.

choices.text: A node and nothing more, since it passes traffic on
choices.why: On the network and moving packets along is exactly what node picks out, and it is as far as the router gets.

choices.text: None of the three: network equipment is a category apart
choices.why: Anything on the network at all is a node, equipment included — there is no fourth box.

prompt: Match each word to what it picks out.
hint: One is about the diagram, one about the machine, one about the destination.

pairs.right: A machine that can be reached and has something prepared to talk
One specific place that requests can be sent to and answered from
Anything on the network, including what only moves traffic along

right_distractors: A machine that has an address but no program listening on it
The path a packet takes between two points on the network

prompt: A machine runs a web server, an SSH server and a mail server at one address. What decides which of them a request reaches?
hint: They share the address, so the address cannot be what separates them.

choices.text: The port number carried with the address
choices.why: The address finds the machine; the port finds the program waiting on it.

choices.text: The operating system reading what was sent
choices.why: The destination is settled before anything looks at the content.

choices.text: The name the client used to reach the machine
choices.why: The name can select a site on one web server; it does not select between services.

choices.text: The order in which the programs were started
choices.why: Nothing in a request could refer to that, and it would change on reboot.

prompt: You try to reach a service twice. The first attempt hangs for thirty seconds and gives up; the second comes back rejected in under a millisecond. What changed between them?
hint: One of the two outcomes proves that something was there to answer.

choices.text: The service came back up, and the program has started listening
choices.why: If it were listening, the second attempt would have been served rather than rejected.

choices.text: Nothing changed; the two mean the same and it is still down
choices.why: They mean different things — one had nobody home and the other had somebody saying no.

choices.text: The machine became reachable, but nothing is listening there
choices.why: An instant rejection is the operating system answering, which means the host is alive.

choices.text: The network improved, so the request now arrives faster
choices.why: Speed alone does not turn silence into a rejection; something has to send one.

prompt: Fill the blank: every host is a ___, and the reverse does not hold — a switch or a router is one without being a host.
hint: The wider category is the one that takes in the machines nobody logs in to.

prompt: Put one complete exchange in order.
hint: Nothing arrives that nobody asked for.
items: The client settles what it wants and where the request goes
The request reaches the endpoint that was waiting for it
The server settles how it went and what to send back
The response arrives and the exchange is finished
trap: The common swap is putting the server's decision before the request arrives — a server cannot decide anything about a request it has not received yet.

prompt: Why does a response report how it went before it reports what is coming back?
hint: Think about what the asker can act on without reading everything.

choices.text: Because a body has to be built before its status is known
choices.why: The status is generally settled first, which is what makes the ordering possible.

choices.text: So the asker can act on it without reading the body
choices.why: A failure is recognisable from the first line, which is the point of putting it there.

choices.text: Because a failed response is not allowed to carry a body
choices.why: It is allowed, and a good one explains itself at length.

choices.text: So the sizes of the two parts can be counted separately
choices.why: Nothing about the ordering follows from measuring either part.

prompt: A request has to carry four things. Which of these are among them? Choose all that apply.
hint: One of the four is about the KIND of asking, not the subject.

choices.text: An identifier for the thing being asked about
choices.why: Without it the other side has nothing to act on.

choices.text: Whether this is a reading or a changing
choices.why: It decides whether the request can be repeated or cached at all.

choices.text: How long the asker is willing to wait for it
choices.why: A real concern, and it belongs to the asker rather than to the request's shape.

choices.text: Context the other side needs to decide with
choices.why: Who is asking, what they read, what they hold — most of a real request's size.

choices.text: The address the answer should be returned to
choices.why: The answer goes back along the exchange that is already open.

prompt: A busy site runs twenty identical machines and sends each arriving request to whichever is free. Which property of the plain shape lets it do that?
hint: Ask what would break if a machine had to remember you.

choices.text: That responses report their status before they report their body
choices.why: Useful for the asker, and it says nothing about which machine answers.

choices.text: That a client may abandon a request at any time
choices.why: That is the asker's freedom; it does not make the machines interchangeable.

choices.text: That the server remembers nothing between exchanges
choices.why: Because each exchange stands alone, any machine can take it — remembering would pin you to one.

choices.text: That a server cannot open an exchange with a client
choices.why: True of the shape, and unrelated to spreading requests across machines.

prompt: An operation is built as six requests, each sent after the last one answered, to a machine 9,000 km away. Roughly what is the floor on how long it can take?
hint: One trip there and back is about 60 ms at that distance.

choices.text: About 60 ms, since the trips overlap on one connection
choices.why: They cannot overlap: each is sent only after the previous answer arrived.

choices.text: About 360 ms: every one of the six pays a round trip
choices.why: Six waits in a row, and no machine at either end can shorten the distance.

choices.text: About 10 ms, since only the first pays the distance
choices.why: Every request pays it; there is no discount for having been there before.

choices.text: It depends entirely on how fast the two machines are
choices.why: Their speed sits on top of a floor that neither of them sets.

prompt: A site is slow. Its machine shows almost no processor use and its queue is full. What fits best?
hint: A machine can be stuck without being busy.

choices.text: Its processors are too slow for the traffic it has
choices.why: Busy processors would show as use, and these are nearly idle.

choices.text: More requests arrive than it can finish computing
choices.why: That would show as work being done, not as an idle machine.

choices.text: The network between you and it is congested
choices.why: Then its own queue would not be full — the requests would not be there yet.

choices.text: It is holding exchanges that wait on something else
choices.why: Idle and full at once is the signature of waiting on a dependency.

prompt: A team doubles the processors on a server that spends most of its time waiting on a database. Which of these are true of that change? Choose all that apply.
hint: Separate doing many things at once from doing many simultaneously.

choices.text: It will do little, because the work was not computation
choices.why: Waiting does not consume processors, so more of them buy nothing.

choices.text: The limit is closer to how many exchanges fit in flight
choices.why: Memory, connections and slots run out before the processors do.

choices.text: Fixing the database would move the number that binds
choices.why: Shortening the wait frees slots, which is where the capacity actually is.

choices.text: It halves the time each individual request takes
choices.why: The time is mostly waiting, and waiting does not divide across processors.

choices.text: It lets the machine answer requests in strict order
choices.why: Ordering is not something processor count decides.

prompt: A search service a site depends on slows from 40 ms to 4 seconds. Pages that never touch search stop loading too. Why?
hint: Something finite is being held while each request waits.

choices.text: The slow service is sending errors that spread to other pages
choices.why: It is answering, just late — and nothing about lateness spreads as an error.

choices.text: The requests waiting on search occupy every slot there is
choices.why: Each holds its place for a hundred times longer, so unrelated requests cannot get in.

choices.text: The machine's processors are saturated by the extra work
choices.why: Waiting is not work; the machine is likely idle while this happens.

choices.text: The other pages secretly depend on search through a cache
choices.why: They may not depend on it at all, which is what makes this failure surprising.

prompt: Your script gets refused after sending requests very fast. What is the most reasonable reading?
hint: Consider what refusing protects.

choices.text: The server is broken and should be reported
choices.why: Refusing is a decision it is making, which is the opposite of being broken.

choices.text: The server is protecting the people also asking it
choices.why: Refusing one enthusiastic client is how the capacity stays available to everybody else.

choices.text: Your requests were malformed and it could not read them
choices.why: A malformed request is refused on its first attempt, not after a burst.

choices.text: The connection dropped and the refusals are an artefact
choices.why: A dropped connection produces silence, not a definite answer.

prompt: Complete the sentence: a server holds many exchanges at once because most of a request's life is spent ___ rather than ___.
hint: One is what it does while a database thinks; the other is what a processor does.

prompt: What does peer-to-peer actually remove, compared with the client-and-server shape?
hint: Look at one single exchange between two peers before answering.

choices.text: The two roles, replacing them with a third one that does both jobs
choices.why: Peer names a machine's position in the network, not its part in an exchange.

choices.text: The need for anybody to answer a request at all
choices.why: Pieces still have to be requested from whoever holds them, and handed over.

choices.text: Only the permanence of the jobs, not the roles
choices.why: In any one exchange somebody asks and somebody answers; no machine keeps either part.

choices.text: The requirement for machines to have addresses
choices.why: Peers must be addressable, or nobody could fetch a piece from them.

prompt: Which of these are reasons the web kept the client-and-server shape? Choose all that apply.
hint: The reasons are about trust and findability more than about technology.

choices.text: An answer sometimes has to come from a particular party
choices.why: Your balance has to come from the bank, not from whoever holds a copy.

choices.text: A shop must be open when a customer arrives
choices.why: An absent peer is tolerable for a film and not for a transaction.

choices.text: What is published has to be correctable afterwards
choices.why: In peer-to-peer, what spreads is what others keep copying, and nobody can amend it.

choices.text: Peer-to-peer cannot work at the scale of the web
choices.why: Large peer-to-peer networks run daily; scale is not what ruled it out.

choices.text: Peers are unable to encrypt what they exchange
choices.why: They can, and encryption is not the difficulty here.

prompt: A peer-to-peer network keeps a list of who holds what on a tracker every client contacts on joining. What does that say about the arrangement?
hint: Ask what part the tracker itself is playing.

choices.text: A hybrid: peers move every file, a server only finds them
choices.why: The tracker waits at a known address and answers, which is exactly the server role.

choices.text: It is not peer-to-peer at all, since a server is involved
choices.why: The transfer between peers is the defining part and it is unchanged.

choices.text: It is fully peer-to-peer, because the tracker itself holds no files
choices.why: Holding no files does not stop it being asked and answering.

choices.text: It proves the roles disappear once the transfer begins
choices.why: The roles are in every exchange between peers as well, in both directions.

prompt: A file is wanted by eleven people this month. Which shape serves it better, and why?
hint: The arithmetic that makes peer-to-peer attractive needs something to work on.

choices.text: Peer-to-peer, since every downloader also becomes a source
choices.why: With eleven people spread over a month there is rarely anybody else online to help.

choices.text: Peer-to-peer, since no single machine's failure ends it
choices.why: Resilience is real and it does not help when there are no peers to be resilient with.

choices.text: A server: with no crowd there is nothing to divide
choices.why: Popularity is what turns downloaders into sources, and eleven people over a month is not popularity.

choices.text: Neither differs, since eleven people is a small load
choices.why: The load is small either way, and one of the two shapes cannot function at all here.

prompt: A payment terminal in a shop sends a charge to the bank and waits for approval. What is the terminal?
hint: Whoever starts the exchange holds the asking part.

choices.text: The server, since it holds the card details
choices.why: Holding data is not the same as being asked for it.

choices.text: A node, since it is equipment on a network
choices.why: True and not an answer: nodes include everything, roles describe an exchange.

choices.text: The client, since it opened this exchange
choices.why: It asked, so it holds the asking part for as long as this exchange lasts.

choices.text: Neither, since it is not a general computer
choices.why: What kind of equipment something is never decides the part it plays.

prompt: Two teams argue. One says their service is a client, the other says it is a server. Both have read the same diagram. What is the most likely explanation?
hint: A diagram usually shows more than one exchange.

choices.text: One of them has misread the direction of the arrows
choices.why: Possible, and it assumes a mistake where the shape allows both to be right.

choices.text: They are describing different exchanges the service is in
choices.why: A service between two others holds both parts, one per exchange, at the same time.

choices.text: The service is misconfigured and is doing both wrongly
choices.why: Doing both is ordinary rather than a fault; almost every service does.

choices.text: The words are used loosely and neither is really correct
choices.why: The words are precise here — they attach to an exchange, and there are two.

prompt: A page shows your order history. Put the four exchanges in the order they complete.
hint: One of them cannot finish until another has.
items: The browser asks the web server for the page
The web server asks the database for the orders
The database answers the web server with the rows
The web server answers the browser with the page
trap: The tempting order finishes the browser's exchange second, because it started first. It finishes last: the server cannot answer until the database has answered it.

prompt: A monitoring tool reports that a machine answers on port 443 but not on port 22. What can you conclude?
hint: Two endpoints, one host, and only one of them is answering.

choices.text: The machine is unreachable from the monitoring tool
choices.why: It answered on one port, so it is plainly reachable.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong with the host; one program is down
choices.why: Endpoints fail one at a time; the machine underneath them is fine.

choices.text: The address changed and only one port followed it
choices.why: An address belongs to the machine, not to individual ports.

choices.text: Port 22 is blocked and the program behind it is fine
choices.why: A plausible cause, and the report alone cannot distinguish it from a stopped program.

prompt: Match each symptom to what it tells you about the far side.
hint: One of the three proves that something was alive to answer.

pairs.left: The attempt hangs and eventually gives up
pairs.right: Nothing was there to say no

pairs.left: A rejection comes back in under a millisecond
A complete answer arrives, and it reports an error
pairs.right: The exchange worked and the content is wrong

right_distractors: The request was never actually sent by the client
The far side is answering somebody else first

prompt: A team moves a page from six sequential requests to one that returns everything. Users abroad notice a large improvement; users next door barely notice. Why?
hint: What was removed costs the same everywhere, and is worth more somewhere.

choices.text: Nearby users have faster machines that hid the delay
choices.why: Machine speed is not what the change removed.

choices.text: The single request returns less data than six did
choices.why: It returns the same things; what changed is how many trips carried them.

choices.text: Five round trips were removed, and distance prices them
choices.why: The floor is the trip; far away it dominates, and next door it is nearly free.

choices.text: Abroad the server is closer to its own database
choices.why: The server and its database did not move.

prompt: You send two requests at the same moment and the second answers first. What should you conclude?
hint: Think about what would have to exist for the order to be guaranteed.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong; nothing ever promised an order
choices.why: They are separate exchanges, and sequencing them is something you build.

choices.text: The server processes requests in the wrong sequence
choices.why: There is no sequence to be wrong about unless one was arranged.

choices.text: The first request was lost and silently retried
choices.why: It answered, so it was neither lost nor retried.

choices.text: Your connection reordered them somewhere in transit
choices.why: Even in perfect order of arrival, the answers may still come back swapped.

prompt: A dashboard updates by itself every few seconds. Which of these could be happening? Choose all that apply.
hint: In the plain shape, the answering side cannot start anything.

choices.text: The page keeps asking, and most answers say nothing changed
choices.why: Simple, works everywhere, and wasteful — the classic arrangement.

choices.text: A line was held open so the server can send along it
choices.why: The client still opened it; the asking simply happened once, earlier.

choices.text: The server reached into the page and pushed the update
choices.why: It has no way to reach a client that has not asked it for something.

choices.text: The data was in the page already and a timer revealed it
choices.why: Possible for fixed content, though it cannot show anything not yet known.

prompt: Fill the blank with one word: which side a machine is on is decided by the ___, not by the equipment.
hint: It is the thing that changes between exchange one and exchange two.

prompt: A colleague proposes serving your company's internal wiki over peer-to-peer, to save on hosting. What is the strongest objection?
hint: Two of the four properties that ruled peer-to-peer out for the web apply hardest here.

choices.text: Employees would each need special software installed to read it
choices.why: An inconvenience, and a solvable one — not what breaks the idea.

choices.text: Encryption between peers would be hard to arrange
choices.why: It is not especially hard, and it is not the difficulty here.

choices.text: Peer-to-peer cannot handle a company's traffic volume
choices.why: The volume is small; peer-to-peer routinely carries far more.

choices.text: A page must be correctable and available when nobody is online
choices.why: An edited page has to replace the old one everywhere, and a wiki has to answer at 3am.

prompt: Which is the strongest reason a server has to sit at an address that can be looked up?
hint: Ask what the other side would have to do without it.

choices.text: Because it needs to be found by people who have not met it
choices.why: A client that cannot address it cannot open the exchange at all.

choices.text: Because a fixed address makes its answers faster to send
choices.why: Speed is not what addressing buys; reachability is.

choices.text: Because the operating system requires one to run programs
choices.why: A machine with no network address runs programs perfectly well.

choices.text: Because clients keep a list of addresses they have used
choices.why: Some do cache, and that only helps after the first successful visit.

prompt: Which statement of the lesson's central idea survives every case it was tested against, including peer-to-peer?
hint: One of them stays true where roles change many times a second.

choices.text: A machine is a client or a server, decided when it is set up
choices.why: The same machine holds both parts in the same second, routinely.

choices.text: Clients are the machines people use and servers are the rest
choices.why: Servers ask other servers constantly, with no person anywhere near.

choices.text: One asks and one answers, and the part belongs to the exchange
choices.why: The last clause is what makes it hold where the parts change fastest.

choices.text: The larger of two machines takes the answering part
choices.why: Size decides how many askers it can hold, never which part it plays.
